item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation I have about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to be minimised. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. I think that framing gets the opportunity backwards — AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team competing against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to make clear that people are interacting with AI, and requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content — including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026, and — following the 2026 Digital Omnibus — generative AI systems already on the market before that date have a transitional period extended to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.
